en: May that ancient jewel of an elephant bring you auspiciousness— he whose quarters of the horizon are made resonant by the clamor of hovering bees sporting amidst the rows of restless waves of the ichor-river, and who, with his jeweled serpents coiled upon his crest-ornaments, has his hoods opened wide by the longing desire to seize the sprouts of wind-blown grass growing from his constantly flapping ears.

There exists that capital city of the Kurus named Hastināpura, which is difficult for enemies to attain; it is the abode of kings whose great arms shine with the splendor of vast sovereignty—splendor like the large pearls of the lunar dynasty—and whose beauty causes the city of the gods to laugh in comparison.

In whose palace, upon the moonlight streaming through the window of the lofty moon-chamber, the foolish folk, because it clings to her body by its very movement, say in delusion that there is a deer upon the orb of the cool-rayed moon due to the soot from the lamp-flame. || 3 ||
In the summer months, when the summits of the city gates are hollowed out by the sun-stones (sūryakānta),
the sign of the lengthening of his days is the lingering of the Sun as he rests upon his path atop those foremost mountains.
Where the stream of water falling from the palace of moonstones— shining with joy at the faces of women—
receives the great renown of "Mandākinī" for the grand festival of the city of the Lord of the Gods.
There, young men perceive night in their minds as if it were day, owing to the blazing house-jewels;
for they hear the deep resonance of the great bell designated by the astrologers to announce every hour.
In that city, women—holding jeweled mirrors as ornaments for their faces—mistook the moon for the face of a beautiful woman;
yet, seeing the reflection in those mirrors, they turned back from such a thought, realizing it was something never before heard or seen.

There, even a skilled musician could not discern the difference between the sound of the lute— whose body was blossoming at the time of conversation and which was filled with the humming of bees attracted by its fragrance— and the sound of the trees in the assembly.
In that city, charming young women, disregarding their modesty before their circle of friends due to the lover’s subsequent anger over a rejected advance,
see his reflection in their inner hearts as if in a mirror and instantly allay their remorse.
In her, the Creator, desiring to display a wondrous marvel among all created women, fashioned a form that lacks a middle;
for from wherever the hips and thighs extend downward, the breasts and other features rise upward in corresponding proportion.
Having descended into the moat, the lotuses encircle the rampart walls on all sides,
as if to conquer with their own luster the faces of all the women dwelling within.

That very region which was formerly raised up by the plow-wielder [Balarāma]—his anger intensified by the offense of the Lord of Karūṣa—as he practiced the art of forceful dragging with his own weapon, appears even today as if it had set out on the path of the Bhāgīrathī to conquer Bhogavatī, which serves as the ornament of his own world.

Having approached that place, Pāṇḍu, of noble prowess, gladdening the minds of his subjects through his governance, led his people beyond reproach by means of the splendors of his fame, which were like friends to the companion of Yamunā (the Gaṅgā). 12.

It is said that the son of Parāśara, whose mind was bowed by his mother’s command to protect the entire land, and who was adorned by the performance of most wonderful ascetic penances, begot [a son] upon Ambālikā, the wife of his uterine brother Vicitravīrya.
Who among men on this earth would not praise his wondrous life-story?
For even though he himself was pale (pāṇḍu), he made everyone attached (rakta) through his own virtue. 13.

The Creator fashioned the moon from the fragments of his fame for the sixteen great gifts—fragments that were perfectly pure and marked by the skins of black antelopes worn within them; thus, the report that the ocean was born from the moon is false.

Intent on subduing the supreme fortunes of others, he who moved with the grace of an elephant seized them with his hands; like the king of birds seizing Kuntī, he took Ramā and the daughter of Madra, whose girdle was the ocean, with the tip of his hand.

Then once, his heart delighted by the hunt, this lord of men mounted a horse whose luster was white as the moon, surpassing all others, and having surpassed the wind in speed; pursued by warriors bearing hunting dogs and equipped with various snares and gear, and accompanied by the two daughters of Yadu and Madra, who were endowed with gentleness and noble discipline, he entered the great forest path of the Himavat, whose majesty is reckoned even by the hosts of Siddhas.

There, with his hair-braid (*dhammilla*) tossed by the finest of the smallest forest *mallikā* flowers, his dagger (*churika*) flashing as it was firmly gripped in his waistband, his gracefulness enhanced by the constant proximity of his quiver, wielding in his hand a preeminent bow intent upon repelling enemies, he—possessing the prowess of the Emperor of the Gods (*Gīrvāṇacakravartin*)—gradually began to slaughter various deer.

A herd of deer appeared before him, as if desiring to conquer by its collective beauty the splendor in the eyes of the two daughters of the Bhoja and Madra kings who were wandering near this monarch. (16)

While this lord of the earth was aiming his arrow at a black antelope warbling with passion, the herds of female deer in the forest spread through the waters of the Yamunā like a single doe, with the tremulous rollings of their eyes directed toward him as he placed the tip of his fingernail upon the mouth of his quiver.
That pale moon caused fear in the young deer of our family, who are like the nectar-rayed moon;
as if out of anger that their own kind was spreading a stain upon him, he struck them with his arrows. 18.
He urged the swift horse here and there; thorns and needles fell upon the king.
Even in the dense forest, he acted like a deer, following the tracks of a boar herd for the sake of capture.
Having immediately turned back from his sport in the mud of the lake at Veśānta upon hearing the sounds of those who were envious of him,
this protector of the earth— unable to endure the sound of the word "earth-protector" (bhū-dāra) applied to those possessing forest-elephants— seems to have brought about their end.
Quickly driving his horse elsewhere himself, that Pāṇḍu surrounded a herd of young buffaloes,
whose elephantine nature was rendered false by their practice of tossing their large trunks forward.
Hearing the neighing of the king’s horses, those elephants of dull intellect became enraged; they thrust their trunks deep into the roots of the Sahya mountains.
Shaking themselves, they buried them for a moment in the nearby trees, yet they were unable to pull them out again for a long time.

Then, saying "Strike!", he simultaneously plunged his curved sword into the mass of buffaloes, while the tips of their horns were brandished by him like the goad of the God of Death standing upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
It was not surprising that he caused the falling of the Candrahāsa sword after his own fall;
for it is only natural that white lotuses should close when they have been nurtured by dwelling in the midst of a forest.
Although this swift horse had already cleared the thicket filled with lions and tigers,
the elephants, intoxicated with rut and dwelling in the caves of the mountains, still pursued him.
Hearing the roar of the expansion [of his bow], the young lions emerged from their caves uttering "hum" sounds;
him he reduced to the state of the five elements (death) with his arrows, not merely at the face, but across the entire body.
On the bank, reclining in secret upon a bed of lotuses resembling a jeweled couch, that Bhīma, being fanned by the breezes of the day’s end, fell into a deep sleep,
surpassing even the excessive languor caused by the abundant fragrance of the flowers.

Then, at the word of his paternal uncle, the son of Pṛthā, placing Hari at the head, set out for the mountain peak named Khandava-prastha along with a multitude of forces, as if to measure their mutual affection. ||1||
When the banner of the Yadu dynasty had departed for his own city, Maya constructed a jeweled assembly hall for the king;
beholding the splendor of which, even now Sudharmā bears life that moves to and fro in grief.
